entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The All India Forward Bloc (AIFB), founded in 1939 by Subhas Chandra Bose — the most charismatic leader of Indian nationalism after Gandhi, who advocated armed struggle against British colonialism and eventually led the Indian National Army allied with Japan during World War II — was the breakaway left-nationalist party through which Bose attempted to build a radical alternative to Gandhi's nonviolent Congress strategy, and today remains a small but symbolically important left-wing party in West Bengal.

Subhas Chandra Bose was twice elected President of the Indian National Congress (1937, 1939) but clashed fundamentally with Gandhi over strategy: Bose wanted an ultimatum to Britain during wartime, using Axis power support if necessary, while Gandhi opposed any cooperation with fascist powers. Bose resigned from the Congress presidency in 1939 and founded the Forward Bloc as his own political vehicle, seeking to unite all anti-imperialist forces.

Bose's subsequent history — escaping British house arrest, traveling to Germany and then Japan by submarine (1940-1941), broadcasting from Axis-controlled territories, and leading the Indian National Army that fought alongside Japan in Burma — made him the most dramatic figure of Indian independence politics. His mysterious death in a plane crash (1945) and the subsequent mythologization (many Indians refused to believe he died) gave the Forward Bloc a martyr-founder of immense symbolic power. Today, AIFB is primarily a small West Bengal party, a coalition partner in Left Front governments, but its historical significance derives from being Bose's political creation.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The All India Forward Bloc — founded by Subhas Chandra Bose as the radical alternative to Gandhi's Congress, representing the militant nationalist tradition that used Japanese alliance against British colonialism, and the political vehicle of India's most romanticized independence leader — is a historically significant footnote in the drama of Indian independence.
